subject: bicycle
pitch: A vintage Dutch city bicycle in mint green. Tall upright handlebars with cream grips and a silver bell, a brown leather saddle with springs, chrome mudguards, a chain guard, a wicker basket on the front filled with sunflowers and a baguette, and whitewall tyres.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a static bicycle model as a TypeScript module, working out realistic proportions like wheel diameter, wheelbase, and handlebar height, and making sure it's oriented correctly with wheels resting on the ground plane and facing forward.

For the wheels, I'm building them from a torus for the tire with a slightly rotated orientation so the wheel plane aligns correctly along the bike's length, plus a thinner rim torus. Since the SDK requires rigid parts to attach to a joint, I'm setting up a single root joint at the origin to anchor all the static parts rather than building out a full skeletal rig, since the bike doesn't need articulation.

Now I'm defining a rod helper for straight frame tubes and picking the color palette — mint green frame, chrome accents, cream grips, brown leather seat, silver bell, and black tires with thin white sidewall rings for the whitewall look.

Working out the wheel details next: dark tire torus, chrome rim torus, and a ring of thin spoke rods connecting hub to rim, plus a short cylinder hub rotated to align with the axle.

Now I'm positioning the wheels along the wheelbase and working out frame rotations so the torus shapes align with the X-axis, then sketching coordinates for a Dutch-style step-through frame with sloping tubes from the head tube down to the bottom bracket.

Continuing with chainstays to the rear axle, then placing the fork from the head tube down to the front axle with symmetric leg offsets meeting the fork crown.

Head tube added as a short cylinder, then building the handlebars with a stem rising from the head tube top, a swept catmull path for the upright bar curving back to grip positions on each side, and cylindrical grips capping the ends.

Now I'm adding a bell as a small silver half-dome sphere mounted near the left grip, then moving on to shape a brown leather saddle.

Positioning the saddle and seat post geometry, then adding spring-like rods beneath the saddle for the suspension detail.

Still working out the spring coil geometry...

For the chain guard, I'm thinking of using an open partial cylinder positioned around the chainring near the bottom bracket, with an arc angle rather than a full cylinder so it reads as a protective plate on the drive side.

Working out the half-cylinder geometry...

Working out the rotation math, I confirm the new y-coordinate equals the original x, so the upper half condition holds. I'm positioning the chain guard near the bottom bracket at roughly (-0.07, 0.28, 0), sized to arch over the chainring's top, but I'm second-guessing whether it might overlap the rear wheel given the wheel's radius and position.

Checking the z-coordinates confirms no overlap with the rear wheel, and I'm settling on a cylindrical, cap-less guard. I'm roughly placing the chainring just outside the guard's thickness, deciding to skip fine detail there, and sketching crank arms as simple rods running from the bottom bracket outward toward pedal positions, though I'm still working out exact coordinates for those rods.

Now I'm working out the mudguard geometry as arcs swept around the wheel axis using rotation math: for a point starting above the wheel center, rotating around the X-axis by angle θ moves it toward the +Z direction, so I'm using that relationship to figure out which starting point and rotation direction will sweep the guard from the rear of the wheel forward over the top.

I'll keep the mudguard as a thin chrome tube rather than adding stays, then move to the wheels: a black torus tyre rotated to sit vertically, with a whitewall ring positioned at a smaller radius along the sidewall face.

Checking the geometry more carefully: at x=0.03 the tyre's radial band spans roughly 0.282 to 0.318, so a whitewall ring at radius 0.285±0.008 mostly overlaps with the tyre surface there, which should work reasonably well.

Now I'm planning the rim as a chrome torus with silver spokes — 16 rods per wheel connecting the hub to the rim in the wheel's plane, generated by looping through angles and offsetting each spoke's rim attachment point slightly from its hub attachment point for a natural splayed look, giving 32 thin cylindrical sweeps total across both wheels.

I'm also designing the hub as a short chrome rod through the center, and thinking through how to build a front wicker basket mounted near the handlebars — likely as a tapered box or frustum shape with a woven texture achieved through a striped paint pattern in warm brown tones to mimic wicker weave.

I'll keep the basket as natural wicker with a simple cube shape plus a rim trim on top edges, then position it in front of the handlebars above the front wheel, connecting it with mount stays down to the fork area, working out the y/z coordinates so it sits clear of the tire.

For the rim, I'm building four edge rods to outline the basket's top opening rather than a solid frame.

Now I'm adding sunflowers poking out of the basket — green stem rods rising from inside the basket up to flattened yellow disc flower heads with brown centers, angled outward for a natural look.

Still placing baguette geometry...

I'm positioning the baguette so it stays within the basket bounds, giving it a tan color with darker score lines and a few cream slash accents on top. Now I'm considering whether the bike needs additional details like brake levers or a small front light.

I'll add a headlamp sphere mounted on the fork crown, then work out pedal placement using small black boxes connected by crank arm rods extending from the bottom bracket in the lateral plane, positioning the pedals on opposite sides of the crank rotation.

I'm also checking that wheel bottoms barely touch ground level given the tire radius, which keeps everything within acceptable sinkage tolerance, and starting to define the seat tube and saddle clamp position.

Now I'm positioning the seat post and saddle above the seat cluster point, then thinking through whether springs should coil around the post or sit as separate rods underneath the saddle to avoid overlap.

Letting the post pass through the coil up to the joint point, then sizing the saddle as a flattened sphere scaled down to a narrow width and longer length for the seat shape.

Since parts without explicit joint attachments just bind to the nearest joint (the root in this case), the rod's endpoints will default to root-joint weighting too, which works fine for this simple rig.

Now I'm setting up the frame joint at the origin and picking colors — mint for the frame tubes and rods, chrome for mudguards — and making sure the needed path/paint helpers like arc, catmull, spiral, and stripes are imported correctly for the wicker texture.

I'm writing helper functions for tubes and wheels: a rod-based tube helper with mint coloring, and a wheel builder that layers a black torus tire, whitewall sidewalls, and a chrome rim with carefully nested radii so they sit correctly inside each other.

Now I'm adding the hub, spokes, and mudguard — using thin rods arranged radially around the hub to simulate spokes, and an arc sweep to form the curved mudguard shape over the rear wheel, while keeping total part and triangle counts well within budget.

I'm now working out the frame geometry: placing bottom bracket, axle, head tube, and seat cluster coordinates, then connecting them with rods for the top tube, down tube, seat tube, chainstays, seat stays, and fork legs with proper left/right offsets for width.

Adding handlebar and grip details...

Placing a small silver bell dome on the left bar end, using a half-sphere geometry kept upright so the rounded top faces outward.

Now I'm positioning a chrome headlamp cylinder near the fork crown, orienting it so its axis runs along Z, and adjusting its placement relative to the front basket and fork legs around z 0.55–0.77.

I'm also checking the headlamp position against the front wheel's radius to make sure it clears, then working out the support rods that connect the basket to the crown area.

Now I'm sizing the wicker basket box and thinking about how to render its texture—a solid tan color might be too plain, so I'm considering a woven stripe pattern to make it look more like real wicker.

I'll give the basket a horizontal stripe pattern in brown tones, add chrome or mint-colored rim rods around the top and bottom edges to tie it visually to the bike frame, then move on to planning the sunflower stems and flower heads that'll sit inside the basket.

Still placing flower parts...

Adding baguette score slashes...

I'm positioning the baguette diagonally across the basket top with one end dipping inside, then moving on to sketch the crank and pedal geometry for the bike.

Adding pedal boxes and a mirrored crank on the opposite side, then working out a cylindrical chain guard arc near the crank hub with a rotation to orient it properly.

I'll adjust the crank rod and pedal to sit outside the chain guard's span so they don't overlap, skipping extras like a rear rack or brake calipers for simplicity, then sketch a chain running from the chainring to the rear cassette.

Still refining small details — thickening the front mudguard chrome a bit, and adding the saddle springs as a spiral sweep from a pivot point near the seat rail with a few turns and thin radius for a coiled metal look.

Now I'm placing the seat post, saddle (a flattened leather-brown sphere), and seat cluster geometry, checking overlaps between the coil and saddle look right, and setting up the head tube positioning next.

I'm confirming the available imports and helper functions (rod, arc, catmull, spiral, stripes, geometry constructors) and checking how joints and bone-weighting work for parts placed with explicit coordinates versus bones. Now I'm sketching a wheel helper function and defining chrome color constants before writing the full build script.

Working through the mudguard arcs for front and rear wheels, placing them along the correct radius and z-offsets, then writing a spoke-generation loop that distributes rods radially from hub to rim using trigonometric placement around each wheel.

I'm now writing a helper function to mirror paired frame elements across the x-axis, being careful that points lying on the centerline (x=0) don't get duplicated when mirrored.

Setting up the module imports and defining the color palette for the bicycle frame...

Still adding frame tubes and stay geometry...

Grip ends should have flat caps for a finished look. For the basket, I'm adding a simple box geometry positioned near the front at roughly y=0.92, z=0.66, painted directly without needing UV mapping.

For the rim, I'm laying out four corner rods forming a rectangular frame at the top (y=1.0) and matching one at the bottom (y=0.84), plus vertical corner posts connecting them, using a mint-colored thin rod radius. I'll set up a reusable ring helper function for these rim loops, and define the basket box to span the corner coordinates matching the rim frame.

Next I'm wiring up mount rods connecting the basket to the bike frame and handlebar, then building a sunflower helper that creates a stem, a flattened sphere for the disc face, a smaller sphere for the center, and an optional leaf, positioning several sunflower heads around the basket front. I'm also adding a baguette rod sticking diagonally out of the basket using a tapered radius for the bread shape.

Now I'm reviewing the remaining bike components — pedals, cranks, chainguard, mudguards, wheels, saddle, bell, lamp, and grips — checking rotation syntax for parts and confirming the chainring disc sits hidden inside the chainguard. I'm also double-checking that helper function signatures like arc, spiral, catmull, stripes, and TorusGeometry are all correct before finalizing and writing out the complete code.
